all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: usability
concepts.definition: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

defining_facts.text: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

The three crucial aspects of the International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 usability definition are that a usable product is intended for a specified group of users rather than everybody, that it supports a specified set of goals rather than every conceivable feature, and that it is designed for a specified context of use rather than all usage scenarios.

The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

concepts.name: prototype
concepts.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.

defining_facts.text: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.

Quick evaluation of design ideas in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle requires both a prototype that models or demonstrates the design idea and can be built quickly, and a quick evaluation method for testing the prototype; both requirements are equally important for a quick execution of the cycle.
Prototyping techniques are used for quick prototyping and quick evaluation of a prototype, and they are typically used to collect feedback on the usability of design ideas.

A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that is used to test whether a design idea will work in practice, so one does not always need to fully implement the idea first.

A prototype can be discarded after it has served its purpose of testing design ideas, or, in the best case, it can be incrementally refined and tested as development progresses until it evolves into the fully implemented final product.

concepts.name: user feedback
concepts.definition: In an interactive system development lifecycle, iterations between stages are intended to account for user feedback, where user feedback means involving users in different ways, not only through feedback.

defining_facts.text: In an interactive system development lifecycle, iterations between stages are intended to account for user feedback, where user feedback means involving users in different ways, not only through feedback.

concepts.name: code testing
concepts.definition: Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing.

defining_facts.text: Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing.

In the coding stage, code testing can reveal issues that require returning to code design, creating an iteration; fewer iterations are preferred because code design is a highly skilled, costly process and late problems are costly to rewrite and test.

The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.
Code testing tests the executability of code by ensuring that the code is bug-free and executes properly, but it does not establish whether the system is usable from the end user's point of view.

The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing.

concepts.name: empirical study
concepts.definition: The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

defining_facts.text: The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing.
The empirical study stage differentiates interactive system development from other software development and is typically not part of other software development in which end users are not involved.

An empirical study broadly has four stages: formulating the research questions, determining the variables after the research questions (without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed and executed), designing and executing the experiment to collect data, and properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the data to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability aspects.

An empirical study, after a system has been fully implemented, is the process of setting up an experiment, executing the experiment, and collecting empirical data for analysis to measure the usability of the implemented interface.

The first stage in an empirical study is formulating a research question, and the experiment is conducted to find the answer to that question, with observations or empirical data collection and data analysis performed based on the question.

never_defined.name: graphical user interface
never_defined.definition: Most standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tools provide drag-and-drop graphical user interfaces (GUIs) that allow developers to create applications or experiences without coding, so users with basic personal computer (PC) skills and non-programmers can learn and use them.

never_defined.name: interface
never_defined.definition: The key characteristics of a user-centric approach are designing interface elements that are acceptable to users, designing layouts that organize elements on the screen or interface to meet user expectations, helping users perceive the system state from their point of view rather than from technical details, and designing interactions that fulfill users' needs by taking them to desired system states, allowing users to get work done by easily transitioning from one state to a goal state.

never_defined.name: interactive system development
never_defined.definition: Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing.

never_defined.name: system
never_defined.definition: A vertical prototype primarily represents interactions or functionalities by implementing a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in practice, in depth from the first screen to the last screen after the last action is performed, not all functionalities, because that would amount to having the full system.

never_defined.name: usability issue
never_defined.definition: In expert evaluation, each evaluator is presented with the prototype, evaluates it independently, and produces a report containing the usability issues perceived by that evaluator; the design team or team lead then combines these reports into a final list of usability issues.

never_defined.name: fully implemented system
never_defined.definition: A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

never_defined.name: text entry
never_defined.definition: The research question 'Is the new text entry graphical user interface (GUI) good?' is problematic because asking several users, for example five users, to judge its quality can produce divided judgments, such as two good, two poor or very bad, and one in between, neither good nor bad, so no answer to the question is likely and no conclusion can be drawn.

never_defined.name: text input interface
never_defined.definition: Research question 2 (RQ2), asking whether a proposed text input interface is better than Microsoft Word (MS Word), elicits somewhat more concrete feedback than standalone evaluation, but it does not give a definitive quality conclusion because 'better' means more or fewer features to different users.

never_defined.name: Microsoft Word
never_defined.definition: Research question 2 (RQ2), asking whether a proposed text input interface is better than Microsoft Word (MS Word), elicits somewhat more concrete feedback than standalone evaluation, but it does not give a definitive quality conclusion because 'better' means more or fewer features to different users.

never_defined.name: standalone evaluation
never_defined.definition: Research question 2 (RQ2), asking whether a proposed text input interface is better than Microsoft Word (MS Word), elicits somewhat more concrete feedback than standalone evaluation, but it does not give a definitive quality conclusion because 'better' means more or fewer features to different users.

never_defined.name: text input task
never_defined.definition: Research question 3 (RQ3), asking whether the new interface lets a user enter text faster than Microsoft Word (MS Word), is less prone to subjective interpretation than a vague quality question because it asks users to complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on speed.

never_defined.name: subjective interpretation
never_defined.definition: Research question 3 (RQ3), asking whether the new interface lets a user enter text faster than Microsoft Word (MS Word), is less prone to subjective interpretation than a vague quality question because it asks users to complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on speed.

never_defined.name: text entry speed
never_defined.definition: Research question 3 (RQ3), asking whether the new interface lets a user enter text faster than Microsoft Word (MS Word), is less prone to subjective interpretation than a vague quality question because it asks users to complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on speed.

never_defined.name: subjective feedback
never_defined.definition: Dependence on subjective feedback is problematic and may not support a definitive conclusion, even for a clear question about which text entry interface is faster, because responses can split.

never_defined.name: objective data
never_defined.definition: An experiment collects objective data for a text entry speed question by having all users input the same text, logging their speed as characters per minute (CPM), and comparing CPM values to objectively determine which interface is faster.

never_defined.name: scientific conclusion
never_defined.definition: A non-testable research question, also called an untestable question, is a question that cannot be directly tested objectively because it depends on users' subjective interpretation and feedback, so a controlled experiment cannot be set up to collect objective data and, generally, a reliable scientific conclusion cannot be drawn.

never_defined.name: generalized concept
never_defined.definition: Research questions should not be framed from generalized concepts such as whether something is good, because such concepts are ambiguous and can lead to untestable questions.

never_defined.name: testability
never_defined.definition: To balance the trade-off between testability and generalization, stage 1 of an empirical study frames multiple testable research questions covering different aspects of a system and combines their conclusions to reach a definitive conclusion about a broader untestable generalized question, such as the overall goodness of an interface.

never_defined.name: generalization
never_defined.definition: To balance the trade-off between testability and generalization, stage 1 of an empirical study frames multiple testable research questions covering different aspects of a system and combines their conclusions to reach a definitive conclusion about a broader untestable generalized question, such as the overall goodness of an interface.

never_defined.name: text entry rate
never_defined.definition: A dependent variable is a variable whose value depends on an independent variable or factor, specifically on its levels; in research question 3 (RQ3), the text entry rate (TER) is the dependent variable because its value depends on the interface, specifically the interface levels.

never_defined.name: untestable question
never_defined.definition: In empirical research, research question framing addresses broader generalizable questions that are untestable by framing multiple testable research questions, collecting objective data for each, reaching a definite conclusion for each, and combining those conclusions to draw a conclusion about the untestable questions.
